title: Capstone: measuring what a recursive call costs
objective: By the end of this capstone you can explain recursion entirely in terms of frames, predict a program's maximum recursion depth from two measurements, and recognise when the compiler has removed the recursion altogether.

blocks.text: Recursion is often taught as a concept requiring a leap of faith. In assembly there is no leap: it is a function that calls a function, and the only thing that makes it work is that each call gets its own frame. This capstone makes that concrete and then measures it.

blocks.caption: Factorial, compiled at -O0 so nothing is hidden
lines: long fact(long n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * fact(n-1); }
sub   rsp, 32                   ; a frame, every single call
mov   qword ptr [rbp - 24], rax  ## 8-byte Spill   <- n saved across the call
mov   rax, qword ptr [rbp - 24]  ## 8-byte Reload   <- n recovered
/* Nothing about recursion is special. It is one function calling a
function, which happens to be itself. What makes it work is that each
call gets its own frame, so each call's n is a different 8 bytes of
memory. The spill of n before the call and its reload afterwards is
the whole mechanism, stated in two instructions. */

blocks.title: The spill before the call is the entire secret
blocks.text: The function needs n after the recursive call returns, in order to multiply. But the call may destroy any caller-saved register, and rdi in particular will hold a different value inside the callee. So n is written to this frame's own memory before the call and read back afterwards. Every recursive algorithm you have written works because of that store and load — the values of the outer call sit in memory that the inner call cannot reach, because the inner call's frame is somewhere else entirely.
Experiment one: how deep can it go
Recursion consumes stack. That statement is usually left there. It can be made exact with two independent measurements and one division.

blocks.caption: Measured on macOS with a default 8 MB main-thread stack
lines: Three measurements, taken separately, that predict each other:
1. Frame size, measured by printing addresses of locals at each depth:
frame 1: this frame is 32 bytes below the previous
frame 2: this frame is 32 bytes below the previous
frame 3: this frame is 32 bytes below the previous
4. Measured, by catching SIGSEGV on an alternate stack and printing
/* 261,448 against a predicted 261,632 -- 0.07% apart. The shortfall is the
frames already on the stack before the recursion started. Three separate
measurements agreeing to within a fraction of a percent is what turns
'recursion uses stack' from a slogan into an engineering quantity. */

blocks.title: This is a number you can use
blocks.text: Once you can measure a frame size and read a stack limit, you can answer a real engineering question: is this recursive algorithm safe on my inputs? A tree walk over a balanced structure of a million nodes goes twenty levels deep and is fine. The same walk over a degenerate structure goes a million levels deep and dies at about a quarter of that. The difference between those two cases is not a matter of style, and now it is a calculation rather than a hope.
Experiment two: when the recursion is not there

blocks.caption: The same functions at -O2
lines: long fact_tail(long n, long acc) { return n <= 1 ? acc : fact_tail(n-1, n*acc); }
At -O2 there is NO call instruction in this function at all:
jne  .Lloop           ; a backward jump: this is a LOOP
And the non-tail version, fact, was ALSO turned into a loop at -O2 --
and unrolled eight times on top of that.
/* Tail-call elimination is the rule that a call in tail position needs no
new frame, because the current one has no further use for itself. Here
the compiler went further and eliminated the call entirely, in both the
tail-recursive and the ordinary version. Recursion depth in the source
says nothing about stack depth in the binary. */

blocks.text: This is the result that matters most for reading real binaries. A recursive function in the source may be an ordinary loop in the binary, with no call, no frame growth and no depth limit at all. Conversely, a function that looks iterative may recurse through a function pointer the disassembler cannot follow. The source tells you the author's intent; only the binary tells you what will run.
When elimination is possible, and when it is not

rows: return f(x)
Often, when the ABI permits
Nothing remains after the call, but ABI, type, variadic, stack-cleanup and compiler constraints still decide whether it can become a jump
return n * f(x)
Only by a stronger transformation
Work remains after the call; here the compiler rewrote it as a loop anyway
Two recursive calls, as in a tree walk
One of them at best
Only the last call can be in tail position
A call through a function pointer
Yes
It becomes an indirect jmp; an unknown target blocks inlining, not elimination
Any call in a function that took a local's address
Usually no
The frame may still be referenced after the call

blocks.text: The last row explains a common surprise: adding a debugging print or taking the address of a local can prevent tail-call elimination and turn a program that ran fine into one that overflows the stack. If a recursive program works at one optimisation level and crashes at another, this is where to look first.

items: Measure your own machine's per-frame cost and stack limit, and predict a maximum depth
Verify the prediction by catching the fault and reporting the depth reached
Compile a recursive function at -O0 and -O2 and determine whether the call survives
Rewrite it in tail-recursive form and check whether that changes the answer
Explain each result in terms of frames rather than in terms of recursion

blocks.caption: How to catch the overflow rather than just crashing
lines: static char altstack[64 * 1024];   /* not SIGSTKSZ: on glibc >= 2.34 it is a sysconf call, not a constant */
static sig_atomic_t limit = 1000;  /* normal run is bounded */
/* the normal stack is gone, so this handler runs on its own.
snprintf is NOT on the async-signal-safe list, so format by hand. */
write(2, buf + n, sizeof buf - n);   /* write IS on the safe list */
sa.sa_flags   = SA_ONSTACK;  /* <- without this the handler cannot run */
/* SA_ONSTACK and sigaltstack are what make this work: the handler needs
stack, and the ordinary stack is exactly what has just run out. The
async-signal-safety rule from the operating systems course applies in
full -- write is on the safe list, snprintf is not, so the digits are
produced by hand. Compile with cc -O0 -o stack-depth stack-depth.c.
./stack-depth is a bounded verification run. Run --exhaust only in a

blocks.title: Compile with -fno-optimize-sibling-calls for the depth experiment
blocks.text: Without it the compiler may eliminate the very calls you are trying to count, and the program will loop forever instead of overflowing. That is not the experiment failing — it is the second experiment succeeding by accident. Being able to tell those two outcomes apart is the point of doing both.
What you should be able to say at the end

headers: The answer your own numbers support
rows: What makes recursion work?
Each call gets its own frame, so each call's locals are different memory
Why is n saved before the recursive call?
The call may destroy caller-saved registers, and n is needed after it returns
How deep can this program recurse?
Stack limit divided by frame size — measured to within 0.07% here
Does a recursive function recurse at runtime?
Not necessarily; at -O2 both versions became loops
Why might adding a print break a working program?
It can prevent tail-call elimination and restore the frame growth

blocks.title: Extend the measurement
steps: Add a large local array to the recursive function and re-measure the frame size
Predict the new maximum depth before measuring it
Raise the stack limit with ulimit -s and confirm the depth scales as predicted
Write the same algorithm iteratively with an explicit stack and compare the memory used
Measure how deep the iterative version can go before its heap allocation fails
State which of the two you would ship, and why, in terms of the numbers
Find one recursive function in code you already have and compute its safe depth
blocks.expected: A frame size that grows with the local, a depth that falls in proportion, and a scaling that follows the raised limit. The final step is the one that matters: applying this to code you already own turns the capstone from an exercise into a decision you can defend — and 'we measured the frame at N bytes and the limit at M, so this is safe to depth D' is an argument, where 'recursion is risky' is not.

cheatsheet: Recursion is ordinary calling; each call gets its own frame, which is why it works
A value needed after the recursive call is spilled to the frame and reloaded
Maximum depth = stack limit divided by frame size
Measured: 32-byte frames, 8176 KB limit, predicted 261,632, measured 261,448 — 0.07% apart
ulimit -s reports the stack limit in kilobytes
A tail call needs no new frame: nothing remains to do after it returns
At -O2 both the tail-recursive and the ordinary factorial became loops with no call
A recursive source function may not recurse at runtime at all
Taking a local's address or adding a print can prevent tail-call elimination
Catch stack overflow with sigaltstack and SA_ONSTACK; use write and hand-formatted digits in the handler — snprintf is not async-signal-safe

checkpoint.prompt: In the -O0 factorial, why is n stored to the frame before the recursive call and reloaded after it?

choices.A: To satisfy the stack canary guarding the return address
choices.B: n is needed after the call returns

checkpoint.explanation: The call may destroy caller-saved registers — rdi in particular will hold a different value inside the callee — so n is spilled to the frame before the call and reloaded after it. That store and load is the entire mechanism of recursion: the outer call's values live in memory the inner call cannot reach, because the inner call's frame is elsewhere.

checkpoint.prompt: Frames measure 32 bytes and ulimit -s reports 8176 KB. What maximum recursion depth do you predict?
checkpoint.explanation: 261,448 measured — the shortfall is the frames already on the stack. Two independent measurements and one division, agreeing to within 0.07%. That is what turns 'recursion uses stack' into a quantity you can design with.

checkpoint.prompt: A tail-recursive function compiled at -O2 contains no call instruction. What happened?

choices.B: The function was inlined into its caller
choices.D: The recursion moved to the heap

checkpoint.explanation: A call in tail position needs no new frame, so the compiler turned it into a backward jump. In the measured example the ordinary non-tail factorial was also turned into a loop, and unrolled eightfold. Recursion in the source says nothing about stack depth in the binary.

checkpoint.prompt: A recursive program works, then overflows the stack after someone adds a debug print. Why is that plausible?

choices.C: It is not plausible; the print is unrelated
choices.D: The print uses too much stack

checkpoint.explanation: Tail-call elimination stops, and the per-call frame growth that had been optimised away returns. Taking a local's address or adding work after the recursive call both remove the tail position. This is the first thing to check when a recursive program behaves differently between optimisation levels.
